extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, critics, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and executing narrative method in novels: choosing and managing scene vs panorama, centre of vision (point of view), authorial distance, scene placement, and how setting and characters should be prepared and rendered. Uses Madame Bovary and other novels as exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic (dramatic) versus pictorial (subjective) rendering
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the scene presented in front of the reader as visible and audible facts (dramatic), or is it 'bathed in the climate' of a character’s mood so that form and colour as they appear in somebody’s thought dominate (pictorial/subjective)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the mode that the story moment requires. Dramatic (scenic) treatment places the reader 'in front of the visible and audible facts' and may be staged without loss; pictorial treatment makes the scene dependent on the character’s perception and mood. Authors may mix modes, but should understand which effect they are invoking (examples: the ball is pictorial in Madame Bovary; the cattle-show is more dramatic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panoramic versus scenic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to survey broad expanses and typical impressions (panorama) or to concentrate on particular scenes and incidents (scenic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage alternation deliberately: some books work mainly as panoramas (Thackeray), others as concatenations of scenes. The panorama gives a continuous, contemplative prospect; the scenic yields immediate interest and specific climaxes. Use the form that best suits the subject and maintain coherence when switching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of adopted method
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist must be consistent on some plan and 'follow the principle he has adopted'; avoid giving yourself more latitude than required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may use multiple resources (dramatic, pictorial, panoramic) but their mixture should be governed by a discernible principle tied to the subject. Unplanned or gratuitous shifts undermine the work; deliberate unmixed methods can be effective for particular themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene placement and preparation (readiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a scene 'at the point where everything is ready for it' so the action is ripe and the place resonant; a scene that is not wanted or fails for lack of preparation is a weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use summary/chronicle to prepare and lead into a scene; ensure that when the scene arrives it 'thoroughly illuminate[s] a new face of the subject and advance[s] the action by a definite stage.' Avoid extraneous scenes that do nothing in particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene as means of opening questions and completing action
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene is the readiest means of starting an interest, raising a question, and later completing what it began (often used for climaxes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a scene to engage readers and recur to scenes at climactic points. Scenes should articulate and resolve, or open the way toward the next stage of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing the centre of vision (point of view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide with which character, if any, the writer identifies and whose mind is revealed; this 'centre' should command the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject can be rendered from a single figure's perspective, limit POV to that figure; avoid haphazard inner plunges. The centre determines how events and setting are perceived (example: Madame Bovary is mainly from Emma’s eyes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize gratuitous POV plunges and manage shifts sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Haphazard and unnecessary plunges into characters' inner lives confuse effect by changing focus without compensating gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift viewpoint only when the subject demands it and ensure transitions are smoothed so the reader is not 'wrenched out' of shared experience. Excessive or unearned changes of focus weaken identification and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguising transitions between subjective and authorial views
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid naked or blatant switches from a character's subjective picture to the author's detached view; do not 'throw off the character' openly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make transitions without awkwardness—use tone, irony, or slight aloofness to keep continuity when the author needs to supersede a character's vision. Abrupt, self-consciously intrusive authorial comments can damage the illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial impersonality and controlled irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an authorial tone that can be slightly aloof or ironic to prevent total identification with a character; irony lets the author step beyond the character’s limited view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the character subjective but introduce a hint of irony to enable the author to provide broader judgment and supply what the character cannot perceive, without explicitly asserting superiority in words. Irony should be implied in tone, not loudly proclaimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensating for a protagonist’s limited perception
rubrics_metrics.description: When the central figure has a feeble or limited intelligence, the novelist must supply additional vision (through other characters or authorial perspective) so the world is adequately revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create other viewpoints within the story or quietly introduce the author’s wider knowledge. Do so cautiously—transitions must not call attention to themselves. Example: Flaubert prepares Charles's mind so the end (his discovery) has force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make setting and secondary characters integral and fully characterized
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the world (town, surroundings, local types) as fully in front of the reader as the protagonist; setting should 'belong to the book integrally.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render locale and minor figures with distinctness and individuality; do not subordinate the town to the heroine as mere background. The environment can be as important as the protagonist in forming the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether the novel’s subject is portrait or drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the book is essentially a portrait (a pictorial study of a character) or a drama (a conflict where events and choices carry the interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is a portrait, emphasize pictorial rendering and characterization; if dramatic, emphasize incidents and how they resolve the conflict. Treatment should follow this fundamental decision (Madame Bovary is pictorial rather than purely dramatic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Early material must justify later effects (foreshadowing and reserve)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include biographical or preparatory material only if it is needed to secure later narrative effects (e.g., Charles’s early life is provided because he is needed for the ending).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid digressions or apparently irrelevant opening material unless they are instrumental in producing a later payoff or in readying characters for important outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events versus illustration: events need not be indispensable
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual incidents may be merely ways of telling or illustrating the subject rather than essential causal nodes in a plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when episodes serve chiefly to illuminate character or theme rather than to drive a plot; this affects how much emphasis and dramatic weight you should give them. Do not mistake illustrative episodes for necessary plot-turning points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layering methods (stratification of techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods may be superimposed—point of view blended with another, pictorial description rendered dramatically, etc.—to create layers and stratifications in treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fusion of methods consciously to enrich texture. Observe how method tends to be laid upon method in successful work and ensure such layering serves the subject rather than showing off technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intrusive, boastful authorial intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not habitually intrude as an independent, self-asserting narrator (a la Thackeray) unless it is a deliberate license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boastful or wilful maltreatment of the story by the narrator can damage the reader’s immersion. If you adopt an intrusive narrator, ensure the licence is consistent with the book’s overall design and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make scenes richly re-readable (density and reserve)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for scenes that 'seem to have more and more to give with every fresh reading'—multi-layered, densely rendered episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft scenes with depth (character, setting, implication) so they reward rereading. This involves concentrated rendering, attention to detail, and ensuring scenes are integral to the book’s structure.
